title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Reduced Mail Service
author: Misty Harris
content:
In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across
the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three
days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them,
each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was "jarring," said Auditor Lori
Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the
11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots
came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost
entirely on [President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who
can vote by mail](https://www.propublica.org/article/trumps-plan-to-restrict-
mail-voting).

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S.
Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots
cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual
deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of
first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer
to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect
after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half
at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice
daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly
for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches
the regional centers.

In this year's primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states
that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California,
Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods
allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as
they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in
counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica's
analysis showed.

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from
what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal
pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for
example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this
year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in
areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica's analysis shows. In
Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the
service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service
as a way to undermine mail-in voting.

"I don't think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter
base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters."

### Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with
Reduced Mail Service

![A bar chart comparing the share of ballots rejected for being late in four
states shows counties with reduced mail service had higher rejection rates
than other counties. North Carolina had an 8.7% rejection rate in counties
where mail service was reduced and a 3.5% rejection rate in counties where it
was not. In Washington, the rates were 5.6% and 2.2%. In Ohio, it was 1.7% and
1.1%. In California, it was 1.6% and 0.8%.  ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/2026-mail-in-ballots-ballot-rejections-
fallback.png)Note: The chart shows the four states where data on all returned
absentee ballots was available. Data from North Carolina and Washington
tracked absentee ballots returned by mail. Data from California and Ohio
tracked absentee ballots returned by any method, including drop boxes.
Sources: California secretary of state, North Carolina State Board of
Elections, Ohio secretary of state, Washington secretary of state. Ken B.
Morales/ProPublica

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general
election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for
these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have [circulated a
memo](https://about.usps.com/what/government-services/election-
mail/pdf/2026-extraordinary-measures-memo.pdf) to the nation’s more than
30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers
should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver
those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency's
longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week
before their states' deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-
track ballots through the system.

"We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair
of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move
swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election
offices."

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told
ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed
directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s
special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.

"I don't think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no
ballots rejected," said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National
Association of Election Officials. "It isn't a question of 'if,' but a
question of 'how many.'"

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024
election ran into problems. An [audit by the Postal Service's inspector
general](https://www.uspsoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2024-08/24-016-r24.pdf)
found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots
correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal
Service spokesperson said "learnings from the pilot" have been applied as the
program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot
rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows
these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. [Research
published in September by the Brookings
Institution](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/postal-network-redesign-and-
mail-ballot-rejections-in-the-2026-primaries/) also found this connection,
projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands
of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including
Washington's 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas
that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may
still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal
Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

* * *

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states
broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself
[frequently votes](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-cast-a-mail-
ballot-in-floridas-primary-despite-spreading-falsehoods-about-mail-voting-
fraud) by mail, and in recent weeks has [started to encourage his
supporters](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1868559110969571) to do so as
well, though he has [claimed without
evidence](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-vote-by-mail-executive-order/)
that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has [mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of
millions of ballots](https://www.propublica.org/article/postal-service-audit-
primary-election-ballots), even as mail volume overall has [dropped 50% from
its high in 2006](https://prc.gov/state-of-the-postal-service).

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited
an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating
overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from [Trump and others in his
administration](https://www.politico.com/news/2020/04/24/trump-us-postal-
service-coronavirus-bailout-206851). (DeJoy did not respond to questions from
ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes
in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the
cuts and the [Postal Service agreed to
implement](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28727902-20211216-stipulation-
and-attached-sett-agmt-for-filing/) special procedures to ensure ballots
weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures
since.

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save
the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in
rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times
were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation
optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4
billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy
agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only
about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

### Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024
Election

A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the
lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes
have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.

![A chart showing the number of ZIP codes that are part of a plan that reduces
mail service. The number rises from near zero in October 2023 to 19,813 in
September 2026, with slow growth during the pilot period, which spans the year
leading up to and just after the 2024 presidential election, and a sharp
acceleration starting in 2025.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/2026-mail-in-ballots-zip-codes-reduced-service-
fallback.png)Source: ProPublica analysis of Postal Regulatory Commission
filings Ken B. Morales/ProPublica

In January 2025, [the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal
Service, warned](https://prc.arkcase.com/api/prc-
dockets/filing/downloadFile?fileId=236113&inline=true) that moving forward
with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as
much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway,
extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they
expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency [put out a
statement](https://about.usps.com/newsroom/statements/010226-postmarking-
myths-and-facts.htm) saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer
for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal
Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and
which wouldn’t.

### Mail Service Has Been Cut in Large Swaths of Rural America

A plan to reduce mail pickup frequency is being rolled out in ZIP codes that
are more than 50 miles from a sorting facility. Areas not subject to the plan
are mostly in or near large cities.

![A map showing ZIP codes where a plan to reduce mail pickup frequency is
active or soon to be active in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. The
plan has been rolled out in most of the Northeast, Midwest and West. Much of
the South is expected to be part of the plan in the future, including large
sections of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, according to ProPublica’s analysis.
ZIP codes marked as not subject to reductions are located within 50 miles of a
sorting facility and are mostly in or near large
cities.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2300-national-
map-static_14fe1d.png)Source: ProPublica analysis of Postal Regulatory
Commission filings Chris Alcantara/ProPublica

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if
it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday
or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO
would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their
ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in
Washington said the Postal Service wasn't direct enough about the fact that
the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

"What they said was, 'We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'" said
Hobbs, Washington's secretary of state. "That was it."

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission
employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped
change their behavior. "That's the part that I think has not been super
transparent about the whole process," she said.

* * *

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states,
which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in
voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail
elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in
ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in
2024, [about
33%](https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-02/2024%20Annual%20Elections%20Report.pdf)
put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the
percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022
primary, ProPublica found.

 _Is your ZIP code subject to reduced mail service? Use[our lookup
tool](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-ballot-delays-postal-service-
midterms#zip-code-lookup) to find out._

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10
cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was
postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the
Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1%
in the 2022 primary.

"It was pretty awful telling people we couldn't count their votes," said
Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. "They were quite upset
because they felt like, 'Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the
post office picked it up and had it.' They felt like it should have counted."

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late
postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service
changes on Savethepostoffice.com, [also found that places in Washington with
RTO had more ballot rejections](https://www.savethepostoffice.com/postmarks-
delayed-ballots-denied-warnings-flash-in-washington/) during local elections
earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off
the alarm bells," he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state's director of elections, said he reached out to
Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers
and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a "total surprise," he
said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more
ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected
by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of
ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election
officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in
the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where
the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the
restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have
also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day
could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines
also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late
ballots in Wisconsin, even though [clerks reported
delays](https://elections.wi.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Wisconsin%20Elections%20Commission%20USPS%20Memo%20and%20Survey%20May%207%2C%202026.pdf?utm_source=vbnewsletters.votebeat.org&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=ahead-
of-midterms-mail-ballot-delays-concern-election-
officials&_bhlid=481eb044045e75e3d8748dd5093f5ffab1cd7aa1) involving mail-in
ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service
changes may have contributed to the delays.)

Wisconsin's data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in
drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure
rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said
Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices
by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.

"If you know that you don't have a grace period, it probably affects voter
behavior," said Patel, the Brookings researcher.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RuralVotingBallots-
Bose6765_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Mail
ballot envelopes are prepared for Adams County, Washington, midterm voters at
a third-party processing center for mail, Direct Mail Enterprises, in Spokane.
Rajah Bose for ProPublica

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the
agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than
expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots.
Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions
to bills, [a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector
general](https://www.uspsoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-09/26-042-r26.pdf)
said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial
reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both
significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for
local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their
destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service
says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to
deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the
primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit
outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large
sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to
Larsen.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote,
concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later
emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

"Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot," she said.

### How We Reported This Story

To quantify the effects of logistical changes at some U.S. post offices on
mail-in ballot rejection rates, we compiled a list of affected ZIP codes and
compared them with ballot-rejection tallies we obtained from nine states.

Not every state tracked ballots the same way. Only Washington, North Carolina
and Oregon tracked rejection rates with enough detail to distinguish ballots
received in the mail from those received by some other means, like a ballot
drop box. In these states, our analysis found a direct relationship between
counties where the U.S. Postal Service’s logistics changes were implemented
and increased rejection rates for ballots sent by mail and received late
during the 2026 primaries. A ballot was considered late if it arrived at an
elections office later than is allowed or was postmarked after the deadline.

In California and Ohio, states with less detailed data, we were able to
connect these logistical changes with increased rejection rates generally,
which experts said were likely tied to the changes at the Postal Service. In
California, data was missing for four counties in the 2022 primary data,
affecting 2% of registered voters. We could not establish the effect in
Colorado, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, the three states we received data for
that do not accept ballots after election day.

The Postal Service does not publicly maintain a master list of delivery ZIP
codes where it has implemented its logistics changes, called regional
transportation optimization or RTO. We compiled a list using filings made to
the Postal Regulatory Commission’s online docket, which gives the addresses of
individual postal facilities that were eligible for RTO. We considered RTO
implemented for any ZIP code served by at least one post office on these
lists. If the filings did not list the post office’s delivery ZIP codes, we
assumed that the ZIP code listed in the post office’s physical address had
undergone RTO. If filings listed multiple implementation dates for a given ZIP
code, we used the earliest one.

Because the U.S. Postal Service does not maintain official boundaries for ZIP
codes, we used ZIP Code Tabulation Areas from the U.S. Census Bureau, which
are generalized areas commonly used to analyze demographics for ZIP codes. A
county was considered to have been affected by RTO if a majority of its
voting-age citizens lived in ZIP codes where RTO was implemented at the time
of the state’s primary. Population data came from the American Community
Survey 5-year special tabulation for 2024, the most recent year available. The
results of the analysis did not change when accounting for margin of error.
Block group data was interpolated to ZIP Code Tabulation Areas. The population
was assumed to be evenly distributed.

The post [Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Reduced Mail
Service](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-ballot-delays-postal-service-
midterms) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
